meta.title: Day 8 Exam: Electrodynamics II — Model Paper 4
meta.subject: Electrodynamics II

glossary.definition: A phasor is a fixed complex number representing the amplitude and phase of a sinusoid at one angular frequency. The common time factor is left out.
Reactance is the imaginary part of an impedance, measured in ohms. It represents the voltage-current phase effect of stored energy, rather than average energy loss.
Impedance is the complex ratio of voltage phasor to current phasor. Its real part is resistance and its imaginary part is reactance.
Admittance is current phasor divided by voltage phasor, the reciprocal of impedance. Its unit is the siemens.
The root-mean-square value is the square root of the time average of a quantity squared. A sinusoid has rms value equal to its peak divided by the square root of two.
Phase specifies where a sinusoid is in its cycle. A phase difference tells how much one sinusoid leads or lags another.

Resonance is the operating condition where inductive and capacitive effects cancel in the input response. For a series circuit the net reactance vanishes; for a parallel tank the net susceptance vanishes.
Bandwidth is the separation between the two half-power frequencies around a resonance peak.

The quality factor measures resonant energy storage relative to loss: two pi times stored energy divided by energy lost per cycle. For a series RLC circuit it also equals resonance frequency divided by half-power bandwidth.
Power factor is real average power divided by rms voltage times rms current. For sinusoidal voltage and current it is the cosine of their phase difference.
Susceptance is the imaginary part of admittance. In a parallel circuit, opposing inductive and capacitive susceptances can cancel.
Wattless current is sinusoidal current in exact quadrature with the voltage. It transfers energy back and forth but consumes zero average power.

cards.title: Question 1
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Show graphically the relation between alternating current and e.m.f. in a circuit containing a pure inductance. Explain the phase relationship between them.
cards.hint: Flip to write a short answer. Draw the graph on paper, then use the rubric to award marks.
cards.recallAnswer: For a pure inductor, \(v=L\,di/dt\). If \(v=V_m\sin\omega t\), then \(i=(V_m/\omega L)\sin(\omega t-\pi/2)\). Current lags voltage by 90°, or a quarter period. On a time graph each current maximum is one quarter-cycle after the corresponding voltage maximum.

cards.q: Did you draw two sinusoidal curves with the correct quarter-cycle displacement?

options.t: Both labelled curves and a quarter-period displacement
Sinusoids shown but labels or displacement incomplete

cards.why: A voltage peak precedes the current peak by T/4.

cards.q: Did you state and justify the phase relationship?

options.t: Current lags voltage by \(90^\circ\), consistent with \(v=L\,di/dt\)
Lag stated without its angle or explanation

cards.why: The derivative of current is proportional to voltage.

cards.title: Voltage leads current
cards.body: Take steady sinusoidal operation, with no added DC current. A pure inductance stores magnetic energy and returns it.

cards.title: Time and phasor pictures
cards.body: The amber voltage curve reaches its peak first. The current peak is one quarter-cycle later. With voltage as the horizontal phasor, current points downward.

cards.title: Question 2
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Distinguish between inductive reactance and capacitive reactance. How does each vary with the frequency of the alternating current?
cards.recallAnswer: Inductive reactance has positive magnitude \(X_L=\omega L=2\pi fL\), increasing linearly with frequency; current lags voltage. Capacitive reactance has magnitude \(X_C=1/(\omega C)=1/(2\pi fC)\), decreasing inversely with frequency; current leads voltage. Their impedances are \(jX_L\) and \(-jX_C\), in ohms.

cards.q: Did you identify the inductive expression and frequency dependence?

options.t: Only the formula or dependence is correct

cards.why: The rate of current change grows with frequency.

cards.q: Did you identify the capacitive expression and distinguish its phase effect?

options.t: \(X_C=\frac1{2\pi fC}\), inverse dependence, lead contrasted with lag
Correct capacitive formula without the full contrast

cards.why: Capacitive impedance is negative imaginary; inductive impedance is positive imaginary.

cards.title: Magnitude versus sign
cards.body: X_C is conventionally a positive magnitude. The minus sign belongs in the signed capacitive reactance or complex impedance.

cards.title: Remember
points: Inductive reactance grows with frequency.
Capacitive reactance falls with frequency.
Both use ohms; neither ideal element dissipates average power.

cards.q: Inductive reactance ____ when frequency rises.
cards.why: X_L is proportional to f.

cards.q: Capacitive reactance varies ____ with frequency.
cards.why: X_C contains frequency in its denominator.

cards.q: The unit of either reactance is the ____.
cards.why: Reactance is a voltage-to-current ratio.

cards.title: Question 3
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: What is the \(j\) operator? Explain its geometrical significance and give one of its applications in the study of A.C. circuits.
cards.recallAnswer: The j operator is multiplication by the imaginary unit, defined by \(j^2=-1\). Multiplying a phasor by j rotates it anticlockwise by 90° without changing its length. It represents phase shifts in AC analysis, for example \(Z_L=j\omega L\), so inductive voltage leads current by 90°.

cards.q: Did you define \(j\) and describe the rotation?

options.t: Only the algebraic definition or rotation is complete

cards.why: Complex multiplication rotates and scales; \(|j|=1\).

cards.q: Did you give a valid AC application?

options.t: A complex impedance or derivative phase-shift example explained
AC circuits mentioned without an example

cards.why: Inductance contributes jωL, while capacitance contributes −j/(ωC).

cards.title: Four quarter-turns
cards.body: Electrical engineering uses j to avoid confusing the imaginary unit with current i.

cards.title: Remember
points: j is an imaginary unit, not a current.
Multiplication by j turns a phasor anticlockwise through 90°.

cards.why: The argument of j is positive 90°.

cards.q: Multiplication by j preserves phasor ____.

cards.q: In the inductive impedance, j encodes the ____ shift.
cards.why: The imaginary factor supplies the quarter-cycle lead of voltage.

cards.title: Question 4
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Using the \(j\) operator, write down the expressions for complex inductive reactance, complex capacitive reactance, and the total complex impedance of a series \(LCR\) circuit.
cards.recallAnswer: For time dependence \(e^{j\omega t}\), the inductor has \(Z_L=j\omega L\), the capacitor has \(Z_C=1/(j\omega C)=-j/(\omega C)\), and the resistor has R. Series impedances add, giving \(Z=R+j[\omega L-1/(\omega C)]\).

cards.q: Did you give both reactive impedances with their correct signs?

options.t: Both \(j\omega L\) and \(\frac1{j\omega C}\) are correct

cards.why: The reciprocal of \(j\) is \(-j\).

cards.q: Did you add them with R to obtain the series impedance?

options.t: Added magnitudes instead of complex quantities

cards.why: Series voltages add as phasors, so impedances add algebraically.

cards.title: A complex sum
cards.body: This is complex impedance. Its magnitude is √[R² + (ωL − 1/ωC)²], not the complex expression itself.

points: Use a consistent exp(jωt) convention.
L contributes positive imaginary impedance; C contributes negative imaginary impedance.

cards.why: The same current flows through each series element.

cards.why: 1/j = −j for the chosen time convention.

cards.q: The real part of an ideal series LCR impedance is its ____.

cards.title: Question 5
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Write down the expressions for the impedance and phase angle in a series \(CR\) circuit connected to an alternating e.m.f. Does the current lead or lag behind the applied voltage?
cards.recallAnswer: The complex impedance is \(Z=R-jX_C\), where \(X_C=1/(\omega C)\), and its magnitude is \(|Z|=\sqrt{R^2+X_C^2}\). Its argument is \(-\tan^{-1}(X_C/R)\). Current leads the applied voltage by the positive angle \(\tan^{-1}(X_C/R)\).

cards.q: Did you give complex impedance and its magnitude?
cards.why: R and the capacitive drop are in quadrature.

cards.q: Did you give the correct current lead angle?
cards.why: Current has phase minus the impedance argument when voltage is the reference.

cards.body: Both signs are correct for their stated quantities. An unlabelled phase angle can conceal a sign error.

cards.title: Question 6
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Why is a parallel resonant \(LC\) circuit called a rejector circuit? Write down the expression for its resonant frequency when the resistance of the coil is negligible.
cards.recallAnswer: At parallel resonance, the inductive and capacitive branch currents cancel at the input, so the source current is minimum and the input impedance is very high. It rejects current at that frequency. With negligible coil resistance, \(\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}\) and \(f_0=1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\); the ideal impedance is infinite.

cards.q: Did you explain rejection in terms of input current and impedance?

options.t: Branch cancellation, minimum supply current and high impedance
Only minimum current or high impedance explained
Claimed maximum supply current or no explanation

cards.why: Large circulating branch currents can coexist with very small source current.

cards.q: Did you give the negligible-resistance resonant frequency?

cards.title: Cancellation is at the input
cards.body: For ideal parallel L and C, Y vanishes at resonance. The finite-loss result is derived in Q20; do not set each branch current to zero.

cards.title: Remember
points: Parallel resonance rejects source current.
The ideal input admittance vanishes.

cards.q: A parallel resonant LC circuit is called a ____ circuit.
cards.why: Its resonant input impedance is high.

cards.q: At ideal parallel resonance, the input admittance ____.
cards.why: The branch susceptances cancel.

cards.q: Branch currents can remain large while the ____ current is small.
cards.why: The source supplies the phasor sum, not the sum of magnitudes.

cards.title: Question 7
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Define the quality factor (\(Q\)-factor) of a series \(LCR\) circuit and give its expression. How is the \(Q\)-factor related to the bandwidth and sharpness of resonance of the circuit?
cards.recallAnswer: Q is 2π times the energy stored divided by energy lost per cycle at resonance. In a series LCR circuit, \(Q=\omega_0L/R=1/(\omega_0CR)=\sqrt{L/C}/R\). The half-power bandwidth satisfies \(\Delta\omega=R/L\), so \(Q=\omega_0/\Delta\omega=f_0/\Delta f\). Larger Q means a narrower, sharper resonance.

cards.q: Did you define Q and give its series-circuit expression?
cards.why: Q is dimensionless and compares energy retention with dissipation.

cards.q: Did you relate Q to bandwidth and sharpness?

options.t: \(Q=f_0/\Delta f\); larger Q gives narrower resonance

cards.why: Use half-power frequencies, where current is peak divided by \(\sqrt2\).

cards.title: Use matching frequency units
cards.body: Do not divide angular resonance frequency by a bandwidth measured in hertz.

cards.title: Remember
points: Q is dimensionless.
For fixed L and C, lower series R gives higher Q.
Bandwidth is measured between the half-power points.

cards.q: A higher quality factor means a ____ resonance peak.
cards.why: Q is resonance frequency divided by bandwidth.

cards.q: Bandwidth is defined using the half-____ points.
cards.why: The current there is I_max/√2.

cards.q: Increasing series resistance makes Q ____.
cards.why: Q = ω₀L/R.

cards.title: Question 8
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: What is the phase difference between the current and the voltage across the resistance in a series \(LCR\) circuit at resonance? Explain voltage magnification and why the circuit is called an acceptor circuit.
cards.recallAnswer: Current and resistor voltage are in phase (as at every frequency). At series resonance the supply is also in phase with current, \(Z=R\), and current is maximum, hence acceptor circuit. The opposite L and C voltage phasors cancel; individually \(V_L=V_C=QV\), so for Q>1 either reactive voltage exceeds the supply.

cards.q: Did you state the phase and explain acceptance?

options.t: Zero phase difference; minimum impedance and maximum input current
Only phase or acceptance explanation complete

cards.why: The reactive voltages cancel at resonance.

cards.q: Did you explain voltage magnification without adding opposite voltages as scalars?

options.t: Reactive drops are Q times supply and cancel as phasors

cards.why: Voltage magnification is not extra net source voltage or energy creation.

cards.title: Large drops can cancel
cards.body: All magnitudes here use the same rms or peak convention. A resistor's voltage is always in phase with its current.

cards.title: Remember

cards.q: A series resonant circuit is an ____ circuit.
cards.why: Its input impedance is minimum.

cards.q: At series resonance, reactive voltage phasors ____.
cards.why: Their magnitudes match and their directions oppose.

cards.q: Resistor voltage and current are in ____.

cards.title: Question 9
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: What do you mean by wattless current? Distinguish between true power, apparent power, and power factor in an A.C. circuit.
cards.recallAnswer: Wattless current is 90° out of phase with voltage and consumes zero average power. For sinusoidal operation, true power is \(P=V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi\) in watts; apparent power is \(S=V_{rms}I_{rms}\) in volt-amperes. Power factor is the dimensionless ratio \(P/S=\cos\phi\), zero for ideal wattless current.

cards.q: Did you define wattless current and true power?

options.t: Quadrature, zero average power, and \(P=VI\cos\phi\) using rms values

cards.why: Zero average power does not mean zero instantaneous power.

cards.q: Did you distinguish apparent power and power factor?
cards.why: Power factor has no unit; apparent power uses VA, not watts of dissipation.

cards.title: Three quantities
cards.body: For a passive ideal L or C, φ is ±90° and the average real power is zero.

cards.title: Remember
points: Real power: watts.
Apparent power: volt-amperes.
Power factor: dimensionless cosine of the sinusoidal phase difference.

cards.q: True average power is measured in ____.
cards.why: A watt measures energy transfer per second.

cards.q: Power factor is a ____ ratio.
cards.why: It divides two quantities with the same power dimensions.

cards.q: Ideal wattless current is in ____ with voltage.
cards.why: Quadrature means a 90° phase difference.

cards.title: Question 10
cards.label: Section A · 3 marks
cards.q: Explain why there is no dissipation of average power when an alternating e.m.f. is applied to a purely inductive or a purely capacitive circuit.
cards.recallAnswer: A pure inductor or capacitor has no resistance, and its sinusoidal current is in quadrature with voltage. Thus \(\bar P=V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos(\pi/2)=0\). Energy enters magnetic or electric storage during part of each cycle and is returned later; instantaneous power alternates in sign and averages to zero.

cards.q: Did you use quadrature to obtain zero cycle-average power?

options.t: Only zero power or phase correctly stated

cards.why: Both \(+90^\circ\) and \(-90^\circ\) have zero cosine.

cards.q: Did you explain where energy goes?

options.t: Reversible field storage and return to source
Claimed that no energy ever moves

cards.why: Instantaneous power need not be zero.

cards.title: Stored energy is returned
cards.body: These energy stores change through the cycle. Real coils and capacitors may have losses; the question explicitly assumes pure elements.

cards.title: Remember
points: Zero mean power is not zero instantaneous power.
Pure L stores magnetic energy; pure C stores electric energy.
There is no resistive dissipation in the ideal model.

cards.q: A pure capacitor stores energy in an ____ field.
cards.why: Its stored energy is Cv²/2.

cards.q: Energy stored by an ideal reactive element is later ____ to the source.
cards.why: The cycle contains positive and negative power intervals.

cards.q: The zero result concerns ____ power.
cards.why: Reactive instantaneous power is generally nonzero.

steps.note: Add the resistive and reactive phasor drops.
The series current is common.

ask.q: Why can the same current be factored out?
options: The voltage drops are in phase
ask.why: Series elements carry one common current.

steps.note: Divide by the complex impedance.

ask.q: What must divide the applied voltage?
ask.why: Dropping the imaginary part loses the phase shift.

steps.note: Choose the source phasor to have zero phase.
Here φ = atan2(X,R).

ask.q: What happens to the impedance phase on division?
ask.why: The reciprocal of e^{jφ} is e^{−jφ}.

steps.note: Read the peak current from the phasor magnitude.

ask.q: Which value does E₀/|Z| give?
ask.why: The numerator is a peak voltage.

cards.title: LR: lagging current
cards.body: For the real-part convention, i(t) = I₀ cos(ωt − φ). Current lags.

cards.title: CR: leading current
cards.body: Here i(t) = I₀ cos(ωt + α). Current leads. Taking imaginary parts consistently gives the corresponding sine convention.

cards.title: Remember
points: Add series impedances as complex quantities.
Divide voltage by impedance to obtain current.
State the real- or imaginary-part convention consistently.

cards.q: In a series LR circuit, current ____ voltage.
cards.why: Its impedance has positive phase.

cards.q: A complex current's magnitude gives its ____ when peak phasors are used.
cards.why: Peak phasors encode sinusoidal amplitudes.

cards.q: The imaginary contribution in a CR impedance is ____.
cards.why: Capacitor impedance is −j/(ωC).

cards.title: Question 14
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: Explain how alternating e.m.f. and current are represented in complex form using the \(j\) operator. Apply the \(j\) operator method to obtain the complex current, actual instantaneous current, and equivalent impedance of a series \(LCR\) circuit.
Did you state a consistent complex representation?

options.t: Complex exponential with amplitude/phase and a stated real or imaginary part
Exponential used but physical-part convention omitted

cards.why: A complex exponential is a calculation device; the physical signal is a specified component.

cards.q: Did you derive the full complex impedance and current?

options.t: \(R+j(\omega L-1/(\omega C))\), current \(E_0e^{j\omega t}/Z\) from loop law
One correct result without a complete argument

cards.why: All three elements share current.

cards.q: Did you give instantaneous current and its phase?

options.t: \(E_0/|Z|\) with \(\cos(\omega t-\phi)\) or a consistent sine and atan2 phase
Amplitude or phase correct but incomplete

cards.why: The phase changes sign when dividing by impedance.

cards.title: Series circuit and current reference
cards.body: R, L and C are all in one loop. Their voltage phasors add, while the same current flows through every element.

cards.title: Loop law to physical current
cards.legend: Use real parts of peak complex signals; X = ωL − 1/(ωC).

steps.tex: E_0e^{j\omega t}=R\mathcal I+j\omega L\mathcal I+\frac{\mathcal I}{j\omega C}
steps.note: Use the element impedances in the series loop.
Factor the common current and use 1/j = −j.

ask.q: What combines in a series loop?
ask.why: Phasor voltages add with a common current.

steps.note: Define signed net reactance X.

ask.q: What is X here?
ask.why: Inductive and capacitive reactances have opposite signs.

steps.note: Use |Z| = √(R²+X²) and φ = atan2(X,R).

ask.q: Which quantity sets the current amplitude?
ask.why: Division by |Z| scales the source amplitude.

steps.note: The physical voltage was chosen as the real part.

ask.q: How do we obtain the chosen physical current?
options: Keep the complex exponential as measured current
ask.why: The same real-part convention must be used for both voltage and current.

cards.title: Remember
points: A complex signal encodes a real sinusoid.
Positive net reactance gives current lag; negative net reactance gives current lead.
At X = 0, the series impedance is purely resistive.

cards.q: The physical signal is recovered by taking the chosen ____ of the complex signal.
cards.why: State real or imaginary part and use it consistently.

cards.q: At series resonance the net reactance ____.
cards.why: ωL and 1/(ωC) cancel.

cards.q: A positive net reactance makes the circuit ____.
cards.why: Current then lags the applied voltage.

cards.title: Question 15
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: An alternating voltage of \(100\,\mathrm V\) at a frequency of \(25\,\mathrm{Hz}\) is applied to a circuit consisting of a resistance \(1.5\,\Omega\) and an inductance of \(0.01\,\mathrm H\) in series: (a) find the current flowing; (b) phase difference between e.m.f. and current; and (c) potential drop across resistor and inductor.
Did you calculate reactance, impedance and current?

options.t: Correct method with an arithmetic error

cards.why: Use √(R² + X_L²), not R + X_L.

cards.q: Did you find the phase difference and state lag?
cards.why: tanφ = X_L/R.

cards.q: Did you compute both element voltages?

options.t: V_R ≈ 69.06 V and V_L ≈ 72.32 V rms

cards.why: These drops combine at right angles.

cards.title: Current and phase
cards.body: The voltage is treated as rms. φ = arctan(1.571/1.5) ≈ 46.32°, a current lag.

cards.title: Phasor check on the drops
cards.body: The large current follows from the small impedance. Do not force the scalar drops to add to 100 V.

cards.title: Remember
points: First find angular frequency 2πf.
The LR current lags.
Use the Pythagorean voltage sum for quadrature drops.

cards.q: The LR voltage drops combine as ____.
cards.why: Their phase directions matter.

cards.q: The angle in this LR example is a current ____.
cards.why: The net reactance is inductive.

cards.q: The stated supply voltage is interpreted as ____.
cards.why: That is the standard convention for quoted sinusoidal AC supply values.

cards.title: Question 16
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: An alternating potential of \(100\,\mathrm V\) and \(50\,\mathrm{Hz}\) is applied across a series circuit having an inductance of \(5\,\mathrm H\), a resistance of \(100\,\Omega\), and a variable capacitance. At what value of capacitance will the current in the circuit be in phase with the applied voltage? Calculate the current and the potential differences across the resistance, inductance, and capacitance in this condition.
Did you use zero net reactance to find C?

options.t: Resonance condition right but numerical error

cards.why: An in-phase current means the series impedance is real.

cards.q: Did you obtain the current and resistor voltage?
cards.why: At resonance \(|Z|=R\).

cards.q: Did you obtain and interpret the reactive drops?
cards.why: Large reactive drops cancel and leave the source equal to \(V_R\).

cards.title: Choose the capacitance
cards.body: This is 2.026 μF, not millifarads.

cards.title: All voltages at resonance
cards.tex: I=1\ \mathrm A,\quad V_R=100\ \mathrm V,\quad V_L=V_C=1(2\pi\cdot50)(5)\approx1570.8\ \mathrm V
cards.body: Q ≈ 15.708. Individual reactive voltages exceed the supply, but they are 180° apart.

cards.title: Remember
points: In-phase current means series resonance here.
Resonant current is limited by R.
Equal reactive voltages cancel as vectors.

cards.q: The variable capacitor is adjusted to obtain ____.
cards.why: The net reactance must vanish.

cards.q: At resonance the current is limited by the ____.
cards.why: The series input impedance reduces to R.

cards.q: The large equal reactive voltages are in ____.
cards.why: Inductor and capacitor voltage phasors point in opposite directions.

cards.title: Question 17
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: Derive an expression for the average power consumed over a complete cycle in an A.C. circuit. An alternating voltage of \(10\,\mathrm V\) at \(100\,\mathrm{Hz}\) is applied to a choke of inductance \(5\,\mathrm H\) and resistance \(200\,\Omega\). Determine the power factor of the coil and the power absorbed.
Did you derive the cycle-average power?

options.t: Multiply sinusoidal v and i, average the double-frequency term, convert to rms
Correct product or final formula with incomplete averaging

cards.why: The oscillatory term averages to zero over a whole cycle.

cards.q: Did you calculate the choke power factor and absorbed power?

options.t: Correct method with one result or arithmetic error

cards.why: Use coil resistance, not reactance, in I²R.

cards.title: Average power from instantaneous power
cards.legend: v = Vₘsinωt, i = Iₘsin(ωt − φ); bars denote a complete-cycle average.

steps.note: Multiply voltage and current at the same instant.
Separate a constant and an oscillating term.

ask.q: Which identity makes averaging straightforward?
ask.why: It isolates the constant power contribution.

steps.note: Average over a full supply cycle.

ask.q: Over what interval must the average be taken?
options: Only the positive half of power
ask.why: A full cycle includes both returned and absorbed energy.

steps.note: The oscillatory cosine contributes zero mean.

ask.q: What is the full-cycle mean of that cosine?
ask.why: Positive and negative areas cancel.

steps.note: The two √2 factors cancel the denominator 2.

ask.q: Which voltage and current values enter VI cosφ directly?
ask.why: For peak values the factor one half remains.

cards.title: The choke is a lossy inductor
cards.body: Use the series LR circuit shown in Q13, with the coil's own 200 Ω resistance.

cards.title: Small power factor, small real power
cards.body: The power factor is lagging. The result is 2.018 mW, not 2.018 W.

cards.title: Remember
points: The double-frequency term averages to zero.
Real choke power is I²R.
Keep milliamperes and milliwatts distinct from amperes and watts.

cards.q: The oscillatory term has a full-cycle average of ____.
cards.why: Its positive and negative contributions cancel.

cards.q: Real energy loss in the choke comes from its ____.
cards.why: The ideal inductance stores and returns energy.

cards.q: A choke has a ____ power factor.
cards.why: Its net reactance is inductive.

cards.title: Question 18
cards.label: Section B · 6 marks
cards.q: A circuit consists of a non-inductive resistance of \(50\,\Omega\), an inductance of \(0.3\,\mathrm H\) and a resistance of \(2\,\Omega\), and a capacitor of \(40\,\mu\mathrm F\) in series and is supplied with \(200\,\mathrm V\) at \(50\,\mathrm{Hz}\). Find the impedance, the current, lag or lead, the power factor, and the power in the circuit.
Did you add both resistances and obtain the net impedance?

options.t: Correct approach with a missed resistance or arithmetic error

cards.why: The coil's 2 Ω is in series with the external 50 Ω.

cards.q: Did you give the current and phase direction?

options.t: I ≈ 3.702 A rms; lags by about 15.755°

cards.why: The positive net reactance is inductive.

cards.q: Did you obtain power factor and real power?

options.t: Only one correct or minor arithmetic error

cards.why: Use I² times the total resistance.

cards.title: Subtract the reactances
cards.body: The series layout is the one in Q14. Include the coil's resistance in the single total R.

cards.title: Current, phase and power
cards.body: Cross-check P = VI cosφ = I²(52). The current lags because X_L > X_C.

cards.title: Remember
points: Total resistance includes wire/coil resistance.
Subtract capacitive from inductive reactance.
Use total resistance for real power.

cards.q: The coil's resistance must be ____ to the external resistance.
cards.why: They are in series.

cards.q: This positive net reactance makes the current ____.
cards.why: Inductance dominates capacitance at this frequency.

cards.q: Real power uses total ____, not total reactance.
cards.why: Only resistive elements dissipate average power.

cards.title: Question 19
cards.label: Section C · 10 marks
cards.q: Obtain expressions for the resultant e.m.f., impedance, and power factor of an \(LCR\) series circuit when an alternating current is flowing through it. Explain the resonance, sharpness of resonance, bandwidth, and \(Q\)-factor in an \(LCR\) series circuit.
Did you construct the circuit and resultant-voltage phasor sum?

options.t: Labelled series loop, quadrature drops and \(V^2=V_R^2+(V_L-V_C)^2\)
Correct circuit or voltage relation but incomplete explanation

cards.why: The reactive drops oppose each other, while the resistor drop lies along current.

cards.q: Did you obtain impedance and power factor?

options.t: Only part of the result correct

cards.why: The angle is the supply-voltage phase relative to current.

cards.q: Did you explain resonance and the acceptor behaviour?

options.t: Resonance frequency without the complete behaviour

cards.why: At resonance the L and C voltage drops cancel.

cards.q: Did you define half-power bandwidth and obtain its value?

options.t: \(I=I_{max}/\sqrt2\) at the edges and \(\Delta\omega=R/L\) or \(\Delta f=R/(2\pi L)\)
Correct bandwidth formula without half-power explanation

cards.why: Half power corresponds to \(|X|=R\), not half current.

cards.q: Did you define Q and explain sharpness with a graph?

options.t: Energy definition, \(Q=\omega_0L/R=\omega_0/\Delta\omega\) and a narrower peak for larger Q
Only formula or qualitative sharpness correct

cards.why: For fixed L and C, lowering R increases the peak and reduces bandwidth.

cards.title: Use the series loop from Q14
cards.body: Draw the AC source, R, L and C in one loop. Choose current rightward in the phasor diagram: V_R is rightward, V_L upward, V_C downward, and their sum is V.

cards.title: Resultant voltage and power factor
cards.body: These are rms magnitudes; the same phasor construction works for peak magnitudes. The voltage leads current when X is positive.

cards.title: From the resonance curve to bandwidth
cards.legend: Fixed source magnitude V; R, L, C positive. ω₁ and ω₂ are the positive half-power frequencies.

phases.name: Response
phases.why: derive current from the series loop

steps.note: Start with the phasor loop law.
Solve for current and square its magnitude.

ask.q: Why is the reactive term squared in the denominator?
options: It comes from the complex magnitude
ask.why: |R+jX|² = R²+X².

steps.note: At ω₀ = 1/√LC the denominator is smallest.

ask.q: Which condition gives the current maximum?
ask.why: For constant R and source voltage the squared reactance is minimized at zero.

steps.note: Power in R is proportional to I².
Cancel V² and rearrange.

ask.q: What defines the two half-power edges?
ask.why: At half power the impedance magnitude is √2 R.

steps.note: The lower edge has negative X and the upper edge positive X.
Solve each resulting quadratic and retain its positive root.
Subtract the two roots: Δω = ω₂ − ω₁; the square-root terms cancel.
Sharper resonance has smaller relative bandwidth.

ask.q: What happens when R decreases at fixed L and C?
ask.why: Δω = R/L while Q is inversely proportional to R.

cards.title: A true normalized resonance curve
cards.body: The plotted response has Q = 3 and shows I/I_max against frequency, with ω₀ at the vertical guide. The horizontal guide is I/I_max = 1/√2; its intersections define the bandwidth.

cards.title: Energy definition and voltage magnification
cards.body: At resonance the total stored energy is constant for the ideal L and C exchange, and the per-cycle loss is I_rms²R times the period.

cards.title: Remember
points: Series resonance gives minimum input impedance and maximum current.
Half-power current is I_max/√2.
Δω = R/L; Q = ω₀/Δω; Δf = R/(2πL).
Higher Q means narrower relative bandwidth, not a different ω₀ when L and C are fixed.

cards.q: The series resonance current is ____ at resonance.
cards.why: Net reactance vanishes, leaving the smallest impedance R.

cards.q: A half-power boundary is defined through current ____.
cards.why: Power in R is I²R.

cards.q: Larger Q means greater resonance ____.
cards.why: The relative bandwidth is 1/Q.

cards.title: Question 20
cards.label: Section C · 10 marks
cards.q: Investigate the behaviour of a parallel resonant circuit consisting of a capacitance \(C\) in parallel with a coil of inductance \(L\) and resistance \(R\) connected across an A.C. source. Derive expressions for its resonant frequency and impedance at resonance, and compare series and parallel resonant circuits.
Did you draw the actual coil-in-parallel circuit and form its admittance?

options.t: C parallel to the series RL branch; \(Y=\frac1{R+j\omega L}+j\omega C\)
Treated all three elements as separate parallel branches

cards.why: The coil resistance belongs in the inductive branch.

cards.q: Did you separate real and imaginary admittance?

options.t: Rationalization started with a minor algebra error

cards.why: Multiply the coil term by its complex conjugate.

cards.q: Did you derive the resonant frequency with its existence condition?

options.t: Correct formula without condition or hertz conversion

cards.why: Here resonance means zero input susceptance and an in-phase source current.

cards.q: Did you obtain the finite resonant impedance?
cards.why: At resonance the imaginary admittance vanishes.

cards.q: Did you compare input response, current and limiting cases?

options.t: Series acceptor versus parallel rejector, current/impedance contrast and low-loss limit

cards.why: For a low-loss tank the source current has a deep minimum near resonance; branch currents need not be small.

cards.title: Keep the coil resistance in its branch
cards.body: The capacitor is parallel to the entire series RL coil. Both branches see the same voltage. Their currents add at the source.

cards.title: Admittance to parallel resonance
cards.legend: R > 0 is coil resistance; resonance here means zero input susceptance. A nonzero real ω_r requires R² < L/C.

steps.note: The capacitor is parallel to the complete RL branch.
Rationalize the coil admittance.

ask.q: Why add admittances rather than impedances?
ask.why: Total current is the sum of branch currents at a common voltage.

steps.note: Zero imaginary admittance gives an in-phase input current.

ask.q: What is the parallel resonance condition used here?
ask.why: The source current and voltage align when input admittance is real.

steps.note: Cancel a nonzero ω_r and rearrange.
The positive-frequency solution requires a positive right side.

ask.q: When does a positive real resonance frequency exist?
ask.why: The squared frequency must be positive.

steps.note: Frequency in hertz is ω_r/(2π).
The imaginary part is zero at resonance.
This is a real, finite input impedance for R > 0.

ask.q: What happens in the ideal lossless limit?
ask.why: As R tends to zero, conductance vanishes while reactive branch currents cancel.

cards.title: Compare the two resonances
cards.body: Series: low input impedance, large source current, acceptor. Low-loss parallel tank: high input impedance, small source current, rejector. Both exchange energy between L and C.

cards.title: A finite-loss precision
cards.body: The derived ω_r makes source current in phase with voltage. With finite coil resistance it need not be the exact impedance-maximum frequency; the familiar peak/minimum picture is a low-loss approximation.

cards.title: Lossless limit and real losses
cards.body: At finite R the capacitor supplies reactive coil current locally, while the source supplies the real loss. The input current is not generally zero.

cards.title: Remember
points: Topology matters: C is parallel to a series RL coil.
Set the imaginary part of total admittance to zero.
ω_r² = 1/(LC) − R²/L² and Z_r = L/(CR).
A low-loss parallel tank rejects supply current; series resonance accepts it.

cards.q: Parallel branch ____ add at a common voltage.
cards.why: Each admittance multiplies the same voltage to give a branch current.

cards.q: The resonance calculation cancels input ____.
cards.why: It sets the imaginary part of admittance to zero.

cards.q: The resistance R in this model belongs to the ____.
cards.why: The coil is a series RL branch, parallel to C.
